# Zvarsity: Modern Portfolio Theory - Correlation Matrix

**Duration:** 10 minutes | **Level:** Intermediate

## What Is Correlation?

The **Risk vs Return** lesson covered how much an asset moves on its own (volatility). **Correlation** measures something different: how two investments move *relative to each other* — whether they tend to go up and down together, in opposite directions, or independently of one another.

Correlation is expressed as a single number, the **correlation coefficient**, always between **-1 and +1**:

| Correlation | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **+1.0** | Move perfectly together, same direction, same proportion | Two large IT stocks like TCS and Infosys |
| **+0.5 to +0.9** | Move mostly together | Banking-sector stocks with each other |
| **0.0** | No relationship at all | A stock and the weather |
| **-0.5 to -0.1** | Tend to move somewhat oppositely | Gold vs. Indian equities, especially in stress periods |
| **-1.0** | Move perfectly opposite, same proportion | Rare in practice for real assets |

The number itself comes from the **covariance** between two assets' returns — introduced in the **Efficient Frontier** lesson as one of the three inputs to Mean-Variance Optimization — scaled by each asset's own volatility so it lands cleanly between -1 and +1 regardless of how volatile either asset is individually. Correlation is, in effect, covariance made comparable across any pair of assets, big or small, volatile or calm.

> 📊 **Figure:** a color-coded correlation heatmap (dark green for strongly positive, dark red for strongly negative) is pictured just below — four illustrative holdings, not your actual portfolio.

---

## A Worked Correlation Matrix Across Asset Classes

A correlation matrix lays out every pair of assets in a grid so you can see all the relationships at once. Here's an illustrative matrix across four broad asset classes an Indian investor might actually hold — Nifty 50, Gold, Indian government/debt funds, and a US/global equity proxy (like a Nasdaq or S&P 500 index fund, increasingly common in Indian portfolios for geographic diversification):

|  | Nifty 50 | Gold | Debt Fund | US Equity (S&P 500) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Nifty 50** | 1.00 | -0.15 | -0.05 | 0.55 |
| **Gold** | -0.15 | 1.00 | 0.20 | -0.10 |
| **Debt Fund** | -0.05 | 0.20 | 1.00 | -0.02 |
| **US Equity (S&P 500)** | 0.55 | -0.10 | -0.02 | 1.00 |

Reading this row by row: Nifty 50 and US equities move somewhat together (+0.55) — both are equity markets exposed to global risk sentiment, corporate earnings cycles, and investor confidence, even though one is domestic and one is foreign. Gold sits mildly negative against both equity markets (-0.15, -0.10) — it isn't a perfect hedge, but it tends to hold up or gain some of the time equities fall. The debt fund is close to zero against everything (-0.05, -0.02) with a small positive tilt toward gold (0.20) — both tend to benefit modestly when investors get nervous and rotate out of equities. The diagonal is always **1.00** — any asset is perfectly correlated with itself, since it moves in perfect lockstep with, well, itself.

Notice that even the "diversifying" US equity position isn't fully independent of Nifty 50 (+0.55, not 0.0) — global equity markets share more in common with each other than a first glance suggests, because they're all ultimately pricing in similar things: global growth expectations, interest rate cycles, and risk appetite. Real diversification benefit comes from the *lower*-correlation pairs in this matrix — Nifty 50 with Gold, or Nifty 50 with the debt fund — not from simply adding more equity exposure under a different flag.

---

## Why Correlation Matters More Than People Think

Here's the counter-intuitive part, and it's the direct continuation of the covariance discussion from the **Efficient Frontier** lesson: **you can add a *riskier* asset to a portfolio and make the overall portfolio *less* risky** — as long as that asset has low or negative correlation with what you already hold. This is the exact mathematical reason the efficient frontier bows the way it does, and it's also the deeper mechanism behind the qualitative advice in the **Diversification Strategy** lesson (Portfolio Basics) to "not put all your eggs in one basket." Correlation is what turns that advice from a slogan into a number you can actually optimize against.

**Simplified example — 2008 financial crisis:**

| Asset | Return in 2008 |
|---|---|
| Nifty Index | -52% |
| Gold | +26% |

A portfolio of 100% Nifty lost 52%. A portfolio of 80% Nifty + 20% Gold lost only about 36% — not because gold is "safer" in isolation (it has its own volatility, as covered in the Risk vs Return lesson), but because it moved in the *opposite* direction when equities crashed, cushioning the blow.

This is the real mechanism behind diversification — not just "own many things," but "own things that don't all fall on the same day." A basket of ten highly correlated stocks (say, ten Indian IT-sector names) diversifies away almost nothing, because they're really one large, concentrated bet dressed up as ten small ones.

---

## The Uncomfortable Truth: Correlations Spike in a Crash

Here's the nuance that catches even experienced investors off guard, and it's worth sitting with rather than skipping past: **correlations between risky assets tend to rise — often sharply, toward +1 — exactly during the market crashes when you most need them to stay low.**

The reason is behavioral as much as mathematical. In calm markets, different assets respond to their own, largely independent drivers — a company's earnings, a sector's outlook, a specific commodity's supply and demand. But in a genuine panic, one factor dominates everything: fear itself. Investors sell what they *can* sell, not necessarily what they *want* to sell, to raise cash or meet margin calls — and that indiscriminate selling pulls asset classes that normally have little to do with each other down together. Historically, many equity sectors that show correlations of +0.3 to +0.5 in normal years have moved much closer to +0.8 or +0.9 during periods like the 2008 global financial crisis or the March 2020 COVID crash. Even some emerging-market and developed-market equities, normally only loosely linked, have moved almost in lockstep during the worst weeks of a global selloff.

This has an uncomfortable implication: **diversification often fails you exactly when you need it most.** The correlation matrix built from years of calm, normal-market data can understate how connected your holdings actually become during the specific weeks that matter most to your returns.

This is *not*, however, a reason to abandon diversification — it's a reason to hold it with realistic expectations. A few things remain true even through crash-correlation spikes:

- **The spike is usually temporary.** Correlations that shoot toward +1 during a panic tend to fall back toward their normal ranges once the acute crisis passes — the 20% Gold allocation in the example above didn't stop being useful after 2008, it went on cushioning subsequent, calmer drawdowns exactly as historical correlation would predict.
- **Some pairs hold up better than others even in a crash.** Government bonds and short-term debt funds, in particular, have historically stayed far more stable than equity-to-equity correlations during panics — precisely because their own volatility is so low there's less room for a correlation spike to do much damage.
- **Diversification's job was never to prevent all losses** — only to make the loss smaller and more survivable than a concentrated bet would have been. A 36% drawdown that recovers is a very different experience, financially and psychologically, from a 52% one.

---

## How the Optimizer Uses This

When the Optimize tab analyzes your holdings, it isn't just looking at each stock's individual risk and return — it builds something like the matrix above across everything you own, then looks for allocation changes that reduce overall portfolio volatility by leaning on low-correlation pairs, not just by picking "safe" assets individually. Two holdings can each look risky on their own and still make the portfolio *more* stable together, if they zig and zag at different times. This correlation matrix is also one of the core inputs to the clustering step in Hierarchical Risk Parity, covered in the next lesson — it's how the optimizer decides which of your holdings are really doing the same job.

This is also the deeper reason a portfolio built this way can outperform a plain index fund on a risk-adjusted basis, even without picking "better" stocks — the index doesn't optimize for correlation at all, it just holds everything in fixed proportion. More on this in the **Beat the Index** module.

---

## Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Correlation Coefficient** | A -1 to +1 measure of how two assets move relative to each other |
| **Positive Correlation** | Assets tend to move in the same direction |
| **Negative Correlation** | Assets tend to move in opposite directions |
| **Correlation Matrix** | A grid showing correlation between every pair of assets in a portfolio |
| **Correlation Spike / Contagion** | The tendency of asset correlations to rise sharply toward +1 during market crashes |

---

## Takeaway

✅ Correlation measures how assets move *relative to each other*, separate from how volatile each one is individually — it's covariance rescaled to sit between -1 and +1.
✅ Combining low- or negatively-correlated assets reduces overall portfolio risk, even if each asset is risky on its own — the same mechanism that shapes the efficient frontier.
✅ Correlations tend to spike toward +1 during crashes, so diversification's protection shrinks exactly when it matters most — but the protection doesn't disappear, and it recovers as markets normalize.
✅ This correlation matrix is the mechanism the Optimize tab leans on both to suggest allocation changes and to build the clustering used by Hierarchical Risk Parity, covered next.

**Next lesson:** "Risk Parity & HRP" — how this app's optimizer uses correlation clustering, not just raw volatility, to allocate your portfolio.

quiz.question: What does a correlation coefficient of -0.15 between Nifty 50 and Gold indicate?
options: Gold is 15% less volatile than Nifty 50
The two assets have a weak tendency to move in opposite directions
Gold has lost 15% of its value relative to Nifty 50
There is no usable relationship between the two assets at all
quiz.explanation: A correlation coefficient near -0.15 indicates a weak negative relationship — the two assets have a mild tendency to move in opposite directions, but far from a perfect -1.0 hedge.

quiz.question: Why might a US equity index (like the S&P 500) still show a fairly high correlation (around +0.55) with Nifty 50, despite being a different country's market?
options: Because both indices contain literally the same companies
Because global equity markets share exposure to common drivers like global growth expectations, interest rate cycles, and investor risk appetite
Because correlation coefficients cannot go below +0.5 for any two equity markets
Because the Indian rupee and US dollar always move identically
quiz.explanation: Even markets in different countries are often correlated because they respond to shared global factors — growth expectations, rate cycles, and overall risk sentiment — even though they're not literally the same securities.

quiz.question: What tends to happen to correlations between risky assets during a severe market crash?
options: They typically fall toward zero, improving diversification
They typically rise, often sharply toward +1, as indiscriminate selling pulls assets down together
They are unaffected by market conditions and stay constant
They become impossible to measure during a crash
quiz.explanation: During panics, fear becomes the dominant driver of selling across many assets at once, causing correlations that are normally moderate to spike toward +1 — exactly when investors are counting on diversification most.

quiz.question: Given that correlations spike during crashes, why does the lesson argue this is not a reason to abandon diversification?
options: Because correlation spikes are a myth not supported by real market data
Because the spike is usually temporary, some pairs (like bonds) hold up better than others, and diversification still reduces losses even if it can't eliminate them
Because diversification guarantees no losses will ever occur
Because correlation only matters for professional investors, not individuals
quiz.explanation: Crash-correlation spikes tend to normalize afterward, certain low-volatility assets like government bonds remain more stable even during panics, and a smaller, more survivable loss is still a meaningfully better outcome than a concentrated one.

quiz.question: You hold only Indian IT-sector stocks, all correlated with each other at roughly +0.85. What does adding one more IT stock do to your portfolio's risk?
options: It cuts your risk roughly in half, since you now hold one more asset
It barely reduces risk, since highly correlated stocks tend to fall together and effectively behave like one concentrated bet
It eliminates sector risk entirely
It has no effect on risk in either direction
quiz.explanation: Since the stocks are highly correlated, they respond to the same sector-wide drivers and tend to move together — adding another one adds very little real diversification, even though the portfolio now technically holds more names.
